JSON: Name: gle_spatio_temporal_pipeline Title: Generalized Latent Equilibrium (GLE) for online, local spatio-temporal credit assignment approximating backpropagation through time Short Hypothesis: Implementing Generalized Latent Equilibrium (GLE) dynamics with neuron-local prospective and retrospective operators causes online parameter updates that approximate BPTT gradients, yielding comparable task performance on spatio-temporal benchmarks while using only local information and linear per-neuron storage. Related Work: Existing approaches to spatio-temporal credit assignment fall into two families: offline adjoint/unrolled methods (AM/BPTT) that compute exact gradients but require global nonlocal information and trajectory storage or replay, and online/local methods (RTRL and its approximations, reservoir computing/ESNs, feedback-alignment variants, equilibrium-propagation/predictive-coding and latent equilibrium) that trade gradient accuracy for locality or reduced memory. RTRL provides online exact gradients but scales poorly (cubic with network size) and requires a dense influence tensor; its approximations reduce cost at the expense of depth and accuracy. Reservoir methods avoid weight updates in deep recurrent layers but relinquish learned representations. Predictive-coding and equilibrium-based models provide local plasticity rules for spatial problems but either assume instantaneous representations or rely on symmetry/time-constant constraints that limit temporal processing. Weight-transport and feedback-alignment address feedback path symmetry but leave residual alignment error and reduced performance for deep/hierarchical temporal tasks. These limitations are: non-causality of offline methods, prohibitive memory/computation for exact online methods, restricted temporal expressivity when forward/backward temporal operators are not decoupled, and open biological/physical plausibility for implementations that require global signals or identical time constants. Abstract: We address the problem of performing spatio-temporal credit assignment in physical, time-continuous neuronal networks using only neuron-local information and without offline replay. We propose a research pipeline centered on the Generalized Latent Equilibrium (GLE) framework, in which each neuron maintains prospective and retrospective canonical variables and minimizes an energy composed of neuron-local mismatches plus task cost. From four principled postulates GLE yields continuous-time neuron and parameter dynamics that implement local three-factor plasticity rules and a real-time approximation of adjoint/BPTT gradients. The pipeline defines algorithms, architectures, baselines and evaluation protocols to quantify how closely GLE updates match BPTT gradients, how well GLE scales, and how it performs on spatio-temporal classification and chaotic prediction tasks. The main contribution is an experimentally testable methodology to evaluate whether prospective/retrospective local dynamics suffice to approximate backpropagation through time with linear per-neuron storage and causal updates. Expected outcomes include quantitative measures of gradient alignment, online performance parity with offline baselines on benchmark tasks, and characterization of scaling and stability constraints. Experiments: Datasets: (1) MNIST-1D: temporally streamed 1D sequences length 360 (interpolated from reference), 10-class classification, 4k training, 1k validation per seed; (2) Google Speech Commands v2.12: 35-class spectrogram stream (use 12-class subset per common split), 37k train, 4.4k val; (3) CIFAR-10: spatial image classification (LeNet-style baselines) for spatial-only ablation; (4) Mackey-Glass chaotic sequences: 30 sequences length 20*Lyapunov time (Lyapunov time λ≈197) for autoregressive prediction, first 10λ for teacher-driven training and last 10λ for free-running evaluation. Baselines: (A) offline AM/BPTT (full unroll); (B) truncated BPTT with truncation windows {1,2,4,8,32} timesteps; (C) RTRL (small networks) and RFLO; (D) reservoir/ESN; (E) GRU, LSTM, TCN (offline); (F) LE (spatial instantaneous limit τm=τr) and predictive-coding allocation. Metrics: classification accuracy on test set, cross-entropy loss, sMAPE / MSE for sequence prediction, cosine similarity between GLE parameter update vector and true BPTT gradient (gradient alignment), memory (peak RAM), compute (wall-clock time per training epoch / per second of stream), online convergence rate (loss vs streamed steps), stability (max/mean gradient norm, divergence events). Experimental setup: implement GLE (continuous-time Euler and RK4 integrators) with mixed-layer architectures: six hidden layers with mixtures of instantaneous and retrospective neurons; two widths matching the paper (≈15k and ≈42k parameters); learning rates and optimizer matched across methods (Adam defaults for offline baselines; SGD/Adam for online GLE with per-parameter η). Seeds: 10 random seeds per experiment. Evaluation protocol: (1) Primary comparison: train GLE online (parameter updates per timestep) vs offline BPTT (batch updates after unroll) on MNIST-1D and GSC; report accuracy and gradient alignment. (2) Ablation study: (a) remove prospectivity (set τr=0) vs (b) set τm=τr (LE limit) vs (c) vary τr/τm ratios {0,0.1,0.5,1,2,5} to measure effect on alignment and accuracy; (d) vary β (teacher nudging) in {0.01,0.1,1.0}; (e) set apical-somatic coupling γ in {0,0.01,0.1,1.0}. (3) Truncation study: compare GLE to truncated BPTT over same compute budgets and measure performance vs truncation window lengths. (4) Robustness tests: add spatial parameter noise to feedback matrices B = W^T + N(0,σ^2) with σ in {0.01,0.05,0.1,0.2}; add correlated temporal noise to input rates (correlation length matching task windows); measure degradation. (5) Scaling study: vary number of layers {2,4,6,8} and width per layer {64,128,256} and measure memory and compute scaling and classification performance. (6) Chaotic prediction: train autoregressive GLE vs ESN and LSTM; evaluate sMAPE averaged over 30 sequences. (7) Diagnostics: spectral analysis of error and adjoint signals (phase and gain), and per-frequency gradient alignment. Report mean and std across seeds. Risk Factors and Limitations: Numerical and stability failure modes: discrete-time integration of continuous GLE dynamics can become unstable for large timestep or for high-frequency inputs due to phase/gain mismatch between prospective and adjoint operators, producing exploding gradients or divergence. Approximation limits: GLE provides only an approximation to BPTT; for signals with dominant high-frequency content (ωτ≫1) the frequency-dependent gain mismatch may misalign updates and degrade learning. Hyperparameter sensitivity: performance depends on nudging strength β, apical-somatic coupling γ, and time-constant distributions (τm, τr); tuning costs increase with network depth. Weight-transport and alignment: practical implementations may require well-aligned feedback pathways or additional mechanisms; misalignment beyond moderate angles will reduce update quality. Scalability: while per-neuron storage is linear, compute for dense layers and long temporal horizons may still be high; very large networks could face prohibitive runtime. Biological/physical mismatch: mapping to spiking neurons or analog neuromorphic hardware may require nontrivial modifications (e.g., spike timing, quantization, device noise) that break theoretical assumptions. Evaluation biases: benchmark datasets and offline baselines favor architectures and hyperparameters optimized for non-causal training; reported parity may not generalize to all problem classes, especially those requiring perfect gradient information or very long-range dependencies. Data and task limits: tasks with extreme long-term dependencies or requiring precise high-frequency gradient information may remain better served by offline BPTT or memory-heavy methods.
